`CONTRIBUTING.md`:

```md
# Contributing

Testers with other GPUs and controllers, people who know the game's internals, and anyone who wants to carry the
scripted runs further through the game are welcome. Three rules apply to every contribution.

## The three rules

### 1. Nothing derived from the game goes into the repository

- No game code, binaries, assets, keys, firmware or save data, and none of what the build makes from them: lifted C,
  function lists, shaders, extracted files, captures, logs. All of it lives in `build/`, which git ignores; the
  `.gitignore` is the firewall, keep it that way.
- Screenshots and captures of the game stay out of the repository too.
- Names are fine: function, class and state names from the game's own executable, used to find places in it
  (interoperability), and coordinates measured in play for the input sequences in `tests/`.

### 2. Clean sources only

- [OdysseyDecomp](https://github.com/MonsterDruide1/OdysseyDecomp) has no licence. Read it as a reference; never copy
  its code, its lists or its files into the repository.
- [ssbu-recomp](https://github.com/Denkishi/ssbu-recomp) (GPL-3.0) is the base of the runtime and the lifter; its code
  is adapted under its licence, and files adapted from it say so in their header.
- Emulator sources and documentation (yuzu/suyu, Ryujinx) consulted for console behaviour are cited where used; copy
  nothing their licences do not allow.

### 3. Every claim is measured

- A claim in a comment, a document or a pull request comes from a test or a measurement, and says how it was
  measured; what was not checked is said too.
- Never change a test or its reference data to make something pass. If a test is wrong, say why in the pull request
  and fix it as a change of its own.

## Ways to help

- Run the scripted Cap Kingdom test (`tests/run_cap_kingdom.py`) on an AMD or Intel GPU and report its result lines
  and the log.
- Play with a physical controller and report what does not work.
- Carry the scripted runs further: the rest of Cap Kingdom (Topper), then the other kingdoms
  ([`docs/scripted-runs.md`](docs/scripted-runs.md) shows how a route is found).
- Speed: occlusion-query results without a GPU wait per report; profiling the game side in Top-Hat Tower.
- Check the shader instructions translated from documentation only (`SHFL`, `AL2P`, indexed `IPA`) against hardware.

## Building

See [`docs/building.md`](docs/building.md), and [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) for how the parts fit.

## Reporting a problem

Give the commit, your GPU and driver version, what you did (or the input sequence), and the run's log
(`build\run\<name>.log`): its last lines name the crash, the missing feature or the stuck state. Never attach game
files or your keys.

## Code

- `runtime/` is C (clang 9), one folder per subsystem (`core`, `libc`, `os`, `fs`, `gfx`, `audio`, `input`,
  `services`, `game`). A new file goes into its folder and into `HOST_SOURCES` in `tools/lifter/build_exe.py`.
  Comments say what the code does and why, and cite the source of any behaviour taken from documentation or another
  project.
- `tools/` and `scripts/` are Python 3.13; `tools/<area>/` for build tools, `tools/dev/` for lookups while debugging.
  `tools/target.py` says where the build's files are.
- Runtime switches use the `SMO_` prefix and are described in [`docs/debugging.md`](docs/debugging.md).
- No game address is written into the runtime: what it needs is generated into `build/gen` (for example `GAME_SYMS` in
  `tools/lifter/gen_tables.py` for game functions the runtime calls by name).
- A change to the shader translator's output must bump `MX_VK_VERSION` in `runtime/gfx/nvn_vk_pipelines.c`, so that
  cached stages are translated again.

## Testing

Say in the pull request which of these you ran:

- **Lifter changes:** `tools\lifter\difftest.py all` (0 different) and `tools\lifter\difftest_mutation.py` (the
  harness still catches planted bugs).
- **Shader translator changes:** `tests\build_mx_equiv.py`, then from `build\bin`: `mx_equiv.exe <folder of dumped
  stages>` (0 different); stages are dumped with `SMO_SHADERDUMP=<folder>` and `SMO_VK_DUMP_MINBYTES=<n>`. And
  `tests\check_all_shaders.py`: every stage of the game's shader files must still translate and compile.
- **System call changes:** `scripts\run.py selftest --env SMO_IMPORT_SELFTEST=1` (0 failed checks). A handler belongs
  to a name the game imports: `--env SMO_AUDIT_DUMP=<file>` lists in its `unimported` rows the handlers registered under
  other names, and each of those has a comment in its table saying how it is reached (the lifted SDK code, a C
  wrapper); the start log has no `is not an import` line.
- **Texture layout changes:** `tests\bntx_layout_check.py` (every texture of the RomFS equal).
- **Changes to the largest-index scan (`runtime/gfx/nvn_vk_draw.c`) or the command-list overwrite index
  (`runtime/gfx/nvn_gl.c`):** `tests\check_fast_paths.py` (`PASS`: both equal to the plain code on random input).
- **Anything that can change game behaviour, rendering or timing:** `tests\run_cap_kingdom.py <new run name>` must
  print `RESULT: PASS`.
- **Renderer, threading or anything a stage, a kingdom or a scenario the scripted run does not reach could meet:**
  `tests\stress_stages.py --save <a copy of a save> --scenarios` starts every stage and every scenario of every kingdom
  (hours, two games side by side; [`docs/debugging.md`](docs/debugging.md)), and its `summary.md` should list nothing
  new.
- **Input changes:** `scripts\run.py padtest --env SMO_PAD_SELFTEST=1` (every check passes).
- **Changes to how `scripts\run.py` limits the test games running at once:** `tests\check_game_places.py` (0 failed;
  starts no game).
- **Changes to the amiibo menu or the NFC reader:** the `SMO_IMPORT_SELFTEST=1` run above (its `nfp` and `amiibo menu`
  lines), and a scripted run that opens the menu and scans an amiibo ([`docs/scripted-runs.md`](docs/scripted-runs.md)):
  the log must show the game reading it (`nfp: the game read the amiibo's model information`).

Known: `SMO_SDK_SELFTEST=1`, the self-test of the service families, fails two checks (the `errno` location is not in
the thread block; `NumberLineAllocator` is not lifted) and stops at `nn::image::JpegDecoder`, which the game imports
but no handler implements.

## Commits and licence

Contributions are licensed GPL-3.0-or-later, like the project. A commit message says what changed and what was
measured.

## Legal

This project is not affiliated with Nintendo. Do not contribute anything you do not have the right to share.

```

`README.md`:

```md
# smo-recomp

A native Windows x64 version of *Super Mario Odyssey* (1.4.1), made by **static recompilation** of the Nintendo
Switch game, with its own runtime and a Vulkan renderer.

It is **not an emulator**: there is no CPU interpreter and no JIT, and no console firmware runs. The game's AArch64
machine code is translated to C ahead of time and compiled for the PC; the system libraries, graphics API, audio,
video, input and file system the game uses are re-implemented by this project's runtime.

> **This repository contains no game code, no game assets, no keys and no firmware.**
> You need your own copy of the game, dumped from your own console. The build reads the dump's decrypted files: no
> keys and no firmware are needed. Everything derived from the game is generated on your PC, under `build/`, and never
> leaves it.

## Status

Early, not finished. Everything below was measured on the development PC (Windows 11, NVIDIA RTX 4090); where
something was not checked, it says so.

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| Start | boot, title screen, file select, Resume: play begins (a scripted start reaches the game's play state at frame 3,564 with the warm shader cache) |
| Cap Kingdom | `tests/run_cap_kingdom.py` plays from an empty save to Mario's first capture in Top-Hat Tower and checks 13 checkpoints against the game's own state: 13 of 13 (42,558 frames), 0 host exceptions, 0 Vulkan call failures, 0 operations not implemented |
| Every stage and scenario | `tests/stress_stages.py` started every stage the game plays as a stage scene (176) and every scenario of every kingdom (100), each from a save made to start there, played for a few seconds at 4x speed: 276 runs, 2.1 million frames, 0 Vulkan call failures, 0 operations not implemented, 0 freezes, 0 audio drops. Cutscenes, the Labo VR stages and the world map have scenes of their own and were not started this way; Luigi's Balloon World and the Koopa races are started by their characters and cannot be started from a save |
| Played by hand | from Cap Kingdom to Cascade Kingdom's first checkpoint, with an Xbox One controller¹; that save continues on 1.4.1 |
| Shaders | every stage in the game's shader files translates and compiles (Maxwell machine code → GLSL → SPIR-V), checked offline by `tests/check_all_shaders.py`: 27,888 of 27,888 distinct stages (7,381 vertex, 20,436 fragment, 3 geometry, 68 compute). The translator's structured control flow equals its reference form on the GPU: 1,519 of 1,519 stages over 6.2 million invocations¹ |
| Picture | the texture layout equals the one Nintendo's tools stored for all 20,203 textures of the RomFS (`tests/bntx_layout_check.py`). 0 frames with a single-frame flash in captures of every frame while the camera pans in Cascade Kingdom¹. The Ruined Kingdom's lightning (a geometry stage) draws: each bolt brightens about 3,000 pixels before the game draws its clouds over it¹ |
| Graphics memory | 1.5 GB at the end of the 12-minute Cap Kingdom run, 2.0 GB in the Cookatiel rematch: textures the game gives up are freed once nothing names them |
| Audio | the game's own audio renderer runs (lifted from its system library) and plays through the Windows audio device (6 → 2 channel downmix, 48 kHz): 0 dropped samples, 0 underruns in the Cap Kingdom run |
| Video | H.264 through Windows Media Foundation: the tutorial videos play with their picture |
| Help | the pause menu's Action Guide opens inside the game window, from the manual in your dump (Microsoft Edge WebView2), and the game waits while it is open, as on the console; checked with scripted input (open, choose, turn a page, back, close). Without WebView2 it opens in your web browser |
| amiibo | F1, or both stick buttons on a pad, opens a menu drawn like the game's pause menu from its own layout textures, fonts and texts: 102 amiibo, in the game's language. The one chosen is held to a virtual NFC reader; checked in Cascade Kingdom: the game reads Peach and runs her help. Mario, Bowser and Luigi checked as well¹ |
| System calls | every system call the game made in the tested scenes is implemented (331 of 331 in the Cap Kingdom run); `SMO_IMPORT_SELFTEST=1` checks the ones written from the game's import list rather than met in play: 0 failures |
| Controllers | keyboard, XInput, and any pad through SDL3 (hot-plug, 8 players, remapping file, rumble, motion): 51 of 51 automated checks with virtual devices; played with an Xbox One controller; other physical pads not tried |
| Window and capture | a borderless window by default; F11 or a double-click switches to borderless fullscreen and back. F12 or a pad's share button saves the frame to the save folder's `album` |
| Save data | journalled like the console's (two-phase commit); the game's autosave and Resume work |
| Speed | 60 fps, paced to a 60 Hz clock: at Cascade Kingdom's first checkpoint 59.8-60.0 fps in each of 20 windows of 300 frames (1% lows 49.4-56.0); the Cap Kingdom run averages 59.4 fps once play begins, lowest 49.5 while the tower stage loads. Development PC only |
| Online | not available: the network services answer as a console without a network |
| Not tried yet | what the 1.4.1 update adds: Balloon World, the new Snapshot Mode filters, the Labo VR mode |

¹ measured on the base game (1.0.0), before this project moved to 1.4.1; not measured again since.

## How it works

1. **Import.** `scripts/setup.py` reads your decrypted dump in place and converts the program's modules to ELF.
2. **Function list.** Every function of the executable, with boundaries from its own unwind tables and symbols (54,214
   in `main`).
3. **Lifting.** `tools/lifter/recomp.py` turns each AArch64 function into a C function; clang compiles them into a game
   DLL. A differential test runs sampled instructions both lifted and in the Unicorn emulator: 23,194 of 23,194 equal.
4. **Runtime.** `runtime/` stands in for the console: threads with the console's three-core scheduling, files and
   journalled saves, NVN graphics on Vulkan with a Maxwell shader translator, the audio renderer, controllers, movies,
   Help and the offline system services.

[`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) explains each part.

## Requirements

- Windows 10/11 x64 and a Vulkan 1.3 GPU (developed on NVIDIA; `VK_EXT_graphics_pipeline_library`,
  `VK_EXT_extended_dynamic_state3`, `VK_EXT_vertex_input_dynamic_state` and `VK_EXT_depth_clip_control` are used).
- Your own *Super Mario Odyssey* dump: the 1.4.1 program, the base game's executable, the RomFS with the update applied
  and the update's control data. [`docs/building.md`](docs/building.md) lists what to dump and how to lay it out.
- [LLVM/clang 9.0.0](https://releases.llvm.org/), Visual Studio 2019 Build Tools (16.11) with Windows SDK 10.0.19041,
  the [Vulkan SDK](https://vulkan.lunarg.com/) 1.4, [SDL3](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL) 3.4.18, the
  [WebView2 SDK](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Web.WebView2), Python 3.13.

## Quick start

```bat
py -3.13 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install lz4 capstone unicorn numpy Pillow
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\setup.py --dump "<folder of your dump>"
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\run.py play --exe smo_native.exe --seconds 0
```

The first build takes a while (lifting and compiling the game); later runs of `setup.py` only redo what changed.
[`docs/building.md`](docs/building.md) has the details, settings and troubleshooting.

## Repository layout

```
runtime/          the host runtime, by subsystem: core, libc, os, fs, gfx, audio, input, services, game
scripts/          setup.py (from your dump to a build) and run.py (start the game, play an input sequence)
tools/target.py   where the build's files go
tools/extract/    the import of your dump (NSO to ELF, version checks) and the function lists
tools/lifter/     the AArch64 to C lifter, the SDK lifter, the differential test and the build steps
tools/dev/        lookups for debugging: disassembly, callers, archives, stage placement, save warps, profiles
tests/            scripted Cap Kingdom run, stage stress test, every shader stage offline, translator equivalence,
                  texture layout, fast paths
docs/             building, architecture, debugging, scripted runs
```

## Plans

- Speed on slower CPUs and GPUs, and shorter stalls the first time a kingdom is visited (its textures and shaders are
  made then).
- Scripted runs further through the game: the rest of Cap Kingdom, then kingdom by kingdom.
- Checks on real hardware for the few shader instructions translated from documentation only (`SHFL`, `AL2P`, indexed
  `IPA`).
- Other physical controllers (PlayStation, Switch Pro) and other GPUs (AMD, Intel).
- What the 1.4.1 update adds: Balloon World, the Snapshot Mode filters, the Labo VR mode.

`docs/architecture.md`:

```md
# Architecture

*Super Mario Odyssey* runs here as a Windows program. Its AArch64 machine code is translated to C ahead of time and
compiled for x64; the parts of the console it talks to (operating system, graphics API, audio, input, files, system
applets) are provided by a host runtime written for this project. Nothing is interpreted at run time.

This page follows the build from your dump to the executable, then the runtime folder by folder.

## From the dump to an executable

`scripts/setup.py` runs these steps in order; each one writes under `build/` and can be repeated alone
(`--only <step>`).

| Step | Tool | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| import | `tools/extract/extract.py`, `nso.py` | Reads your decrypted dump in place. The program's modules (`main`, `sdk`, `subsdk0`, `rtld`) are NSO files: their segments are LZ4-decompressed into ELF images in `build/dump/update/elf`. The base game's `main` goes to `build/dump/base`. Each piece is checked by what it contains: the program id in `main.npdm`, the NintendoSDK version the modules carry (7.3.2; the base game's 3.5.1), the display version in `control.nacp` (1.4.1). `build/romfs` and `build/manual` become directory junctions to your dump, so the 5.7 GB RomFS is read where it is. |
| functions | `tools/extract/functions.py` | Every function of every module with exact boundaries, from the `.eh_frame` unwind tables and the sized symbols, never from guesses: 54,214 functions in `main`. Names come from the module's symbols and, for the game's state classes, from its RTTI (the 1.4.1 `main` keeps almost no symbols). |
| lift | `tools/lifter/recomp.py` | Each AArch64 function becomes one C function working on a register context (`Ctx`, `runtime/core/runtime.h`). Direct calls stay direct C calls; indirect calls go through the runtime's dispatcher; calls into other modules go to the runtime's handlers. Floating point follows the console's rules exactly (`fpexact.h`), and NEON vector instructions have C helpers (`neon.h`). |
| compile | `tools/lifter/build_main.py` | clang 9 compiles the lifted C (`-O1`, with a time limit per file that falls back to unoptimised code for the largest functions) into `smo_game.dll`. The lifted code is a DLL of its own so the runtime, which changes far more often, links in seconds. |
| tables | `tools/lifter/gen_tables.py` | Writes `build/gen/image.h`: the image layout, relocations, dynamic symbols, and the addresses of the few game functions the runtime calls or watches. The update's stripped `main` gets those by matching against the base game's `main`, whose symbols name them. No game address is written in the runtime's sources. |
| sdk | `tools/lifter/sdklift.py` | Lifts parts of the game's own SDK module the same way (1,609 functions: the audio renderer and its DSP, allocators, the vibration player, ...). `tools/lifter/sdklift_rules.txt` chooses the roots and the points where the host answers instead. |
| link | `tools/lifter/build_exe.py` | Compiles the host runtime and links `build/bin/smo_native.exe`; builds `smo_glslang.dll` (GLSL to SPIR-V through the Vulkan SDK's shaderc). |
| check | `tools/lifter/difftest.py`, `linkcheck.py` | The lifter's differential test: sampled instruction shapes run both as lifted C and in the Unicorn emulator, from random, special floating-point, branch and trap states; registers, flags and memory must match (23,194 of 23,194). `difftest_mutation.py` checks that the test catches planted bugs. |

## The runtime

`runtime/` is C, compiled with clang 9. Each folder is one area of the console; files include each other's headers
by name (every folder is an include directory).

### `core/`: loading and calling

- `boot.c` runs the game's own start-up: `nninitStartup`, the static constructors, `nnMain`.
- `hostrt.c` maps the image at 0x7100000000 (addresses in comments are offsets from there), applies its relocations,
  makes code and constants read-only, and dispatches indirect calls (a hash table from guest address to lifted
  function) and calls to imported functions (by name, to the handler registered for it). On a crash it prints the guest
  function, its registers and the host call stack. `SMO_STRICT=1` lists the imports whose handler does nothing.
- `gamedll.c` and `game_shim.c` join the exe and `smo_game.dll`.
- `sdklift_rt.c` maps the SDK module beside the game, so lifted SDK code finds its own data.
- `hitch.c`: the hitch log (`SMO_HITCH`), which says which thread was late in a slow frame and inside what.

### `libc/`: the C and C++ runtime

The C library, the C++ standard library pieces the game imports, the C++ ABI runtime (exceptions, RTTI, guard
variables) and the unwinder that walks the guest stack with the game's unwind tables.

### `os/`: threads, time, memory

- `os_threads.c`: `nn::os` threads, events, message queues and the console's scheduling. The console has three cores
  and runs only the highest-priority ready thread of each; three processors of the PC stand for them, every guest
  thread keeps its core mask, and the game's priorities keep their order. The game depends on this: with free
  scheduling 4 of 6 boots failed in its heap code while loading, with the model 0 of 6.
- `nntime.c`: clocks, calendar time and time zones (from Windows, or the public tz database when present).
- `smo_nn.c`: the memory heap the game's allocators sit on (a pagefile-backed section, so graphics memory pools can
  show the same pages at a second address) and SDK functions no other table handles.
- `nnsdk.c`, `nnmisc.c`: smaller SDK families.

### `fs/`: files and saves

`nn::fs` on host folders. The RomFS is read-only from `build/romfs`; save data lives in the user folder and is
journalled like the console's: a commit writes the new files beside the old ones, then switches over, so a process
killed in either phase leaves a whole save.

### `gfx/`: graphics

- `nvn_stub.c` hands out an entry point for every NVN function the game asks for; `nvn_gl.c` is the front end:
  command lists are recorded on the game's threads and replayed by one render thread, and a recorded list lives until
  the game finalizes it or records over its memory, as on the console.
- The Vulkan back end, the default: `nvn_vk.c` (device, swapchain, present), `nvn_vk_draw.c` (draws, textures, copies,
  the stream ring that copies guest memory to the GPU), `nvn_vk_pipelines.c` (shader stages and pipelines, made ahead
  of the draw by worker threads), `nvn_vk_watchdog.c` (a report of every thread when no frame comes for 5 seconds).
  The OpenGL back end in `nvn_gl.c` is older and kept as a fallback (`renderer = opengl`, NVIDIA only).
- `mx_translate.c` translates Maxwell shader machine code into GLSL with structured control flow; `smo_glslang.dll`
  (`vk_shaderc_shim.c`) compiles it to SPIR-V. Translated stages are cached in `build/cache/vk`.
- `tex_decode.c`: NVN texture formats, the Tegra block-linear layout, BCn and ASTC decoding. `nvn_layout.c` answers the
  driver's texture size and alignment queries from the same layout rules.
- `display.c`: the window, and the one 60 Hz clock that paces both the game's vsync event and the presents.
  `gfx_options.c` reads `graphics.ini`.

### `audio/`

The game's audio renderer, including its DSP command processing, is lifted SDK code; `smo_audio.c` supplies what lies
below the SDK on a console (the renderer's clock and the output device, with a 6 to 2 channel downmix). `nnaudio.c`:
the answers to two audio-device imports, for a run in which the lifted SDK code does not replace them.

### `input/`

`nnhid.c` is `nn::hid`: controllers, motion, vibration, and the input sequences of scripted runs (`SMO_SEQ`).
`nnpad_sdl.c` reads the keyboard, XInput and every pad SDL3 knows, with hot-plug and a remapping file
(`controllers.ini`).

### `services/`: system services and applets

The offline console: web pages and Help (`nnapplet.c`), the NFC reader that amiibo are held to, the Capture button's
pictures in the album folder (`nnalbum.c`), sockets on Winsock without TLS (`nnnet.c`, `nnsocket.inc`), the online services answering
as a console without a network (`nnonline.inc`), the shared fonts (`nnpl.c`) and the font engine that draws them
(`nnfontll.c`), the movie player on Windows Media Foundation (`nnmovie_mf.c`). `nnservices.c` registers these families
and runs their self-test (`SMO_SDK_SELFTEST=1`).

### `game/`: features of this game

- `smo_nerve.c`: names the state each of the game's state machines is in (its "nerves", from RTTI), so scripted runs
  can wait for states and the log can show them; also starts stages and lists of stages for tests.
- `smo_amiibo.c`, `smo_ui.c`: the amiibo menu, drawn in software from the game's own layout textures, fonts and
  messages.
- `smo_guide.c`: the game's Help shown inside the game window (Microsoft Edge WebView2).
- `smo_fast.c`: host code in place of a hot game function (the sort of the sampler list), with a check mode that
  compares both.
- `smo_selftest.c`: `SMO_IMPORT_SELFTEST=1`, a check of the handlers written from the game's import list rather than
  met in play.

## Files at run time

The game runs from `build/bin`; its paths are relative to it:

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `build/romfs`, `build/manual` | the game's files and its Help pages (junctions to your dump) |
| `build/sysdata/fonts` | the console's shared fonts, when you dumped them; otherwise free fonts from `deps/fonts`, then Windows' own |
| `build/config` | `graphics.ini` and `controllers.ini`, written with documented defaults on the first start |
| `build/userdata` | save data and the album; `scripts/run.py --userdata` points a run at another folder |
| `build/cache/vk` | translated shader stages and the driver's pipeline cache |
| `build/run` | logs of runs started with `scripts/run.py` |

## Reading the sources

Comments say where a behaviour comes from:

- `[game 0x...]`: an offset in the game's `main`; `[sdk 7.3.2 0x...]`: in the game's SDK module.
- `[sdk]` with NintendoSDK 3.5.1, where the file says so: the base game's SDK module.
- `[doc]`, `[suyu]`: public documentation and emulator sources, by file.
- Files adapted from [ssbu-recomp](https://github.com/Denkishi/ssbu-recomp) keep the addresses that project read in
  *Super Smash Bros. Ultimate* 13.0.4's modules, and their headers say so. Addresses of the form 0x71xxxxxxxx above
  0x7102000000 are always from there: this game's `main` is smaller.
- A number in a comment comes from a measurement or a test, which the comment names.

`docs/building.md`:

```md
# Building

Everything the build makes from the game is derived from **your own dump** on **your own PC**, into `build/` (ignored
by git). One script does all of it, in steps that resume where they stopped:

```bat
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\setup.py --dump "<folder of your dump>"
```

No console keys and no firmware are needed: the dump's files are already decrypted by your console, and the build only
converts and reads them.

## What you need

- Windows 10/11 x64 and a GPU with Vulkan 1.3 (developed on NVIDIA). The renderer uses
  `VK_EXT_graphics_pipeline_library`, `VK_EXT_extended_dynamic_state3`, `VK_EXT_vertex_input_dynamic_state` and
  `VK_EXT_depth_clip_control`.
- **Python 3.13** in a virtual environment in the repository:
  ```bat
  py -3.13 -m venv .venv
  .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install lz4 capstone unicorn numpy Pillow
  ```
- **LLVM/clang 9.0.0** (the lifted code is compiled with it): unpack it to `C:\llvm-9.0.0` or point `LLVM_ROOT` at it.
- **Visual Studio 2019 Build Tools** (16.11) with the Windows SDK 10.0.19041: the C runtime and system libraries clang
  links against.
- The **Vulkan SDK** 1.4: its headers and `vulkan-1.lib`, and its `shaderc_shared.dll`, which `smo_glslang.dll` (built
  from `runtime/gfx/vk_shaderc_shim.c`) uses to turn GLSL into SPIR-V. `VULKAN_HEADERS` overrides the header folder.
- **SDL3** 3.4.18 (the development package for Visual C++) in `deps\SDL3-3.4.18`, or `SDL3_ROOT` pointing at it.
- The **WebView2 SDK** (Microsoft's NuGet package `Microsoft.Web.WebView2`, developed with 1.0.2903.40; a `.nupkg` is
  a zip file): its `build\native\include` and `build\native\x64` folders in `deps\webview2-<version>\build\native\`, or
  `WEBVIEW2_ROOT` pointing at the unpacked package. The game's Help is shown in the game window with it; the **WebView2
  Runtime** it needs is part of Windows 11 (on Windows 10, install Microsoft's Evergreen WebView2 Runtime). Without the
  runtime, Help opens in your web browser.

`scripts\setup.py` checks for each of these first and names what is missing.

## What to dump

Dump the game from your own console with a homebrew dumping tool that writes decrypted files, such as nxdumptool. The
build needs the game as the 1.4.1 update leaves it, plus the base game's executable, in one folder laid out like this:

```
<your dump folder>\
  exefs\          the program's ExeFS with the 1.4.1 update: main, main.npdm, sdk, rtld, subsdk0
  exefs-1.0.0\    the base game's ExeFS, or only its main (exefs-base\ is accepted too)
  romfs\          the game's RomFS with the 1.4.1 update applied
  control.nacp    the update's control data
  manual\         optional: the Help pages (the RomFS of the game's HTML document content: html-document\...)
  fonts\          optional: the console's shared fonts, as the console stores them (nintendo_udsg-r_std_003.bfttf
                  and the others) or as .ttf files of the same names
```

- **Why the base game's `main`:** the update's executable keeps almost no symbols. The base game's does, and the few
  functions the runtime needs by name are found in the update's by matching them with the base game's.
- **Checks:** the import reads the program id from `main.npdm`, the NintendoSDK version the modules were built with
  (7.3.2 for 1.4.1, 3.5.1 for the base game) and the display version in `control.nacp` (1.4.1), and looks for the
  RomFS's own folders. A missing or wrong piece is named.
- **Read in place:** `build\romfs` and `build\manual` become directory junctions to your dump's folders (the RomFS is
  about 5.7 GB), so keep the dump where it is. Only the executable modules are converted, into `build\dump`.
- **Fonts:** the game draws with the console's shared fonts in one place met so far, the map screen's legend and its
  travel-guide pages. Without `fonts\`, free fonts stand in: put Noto Sans (and Noto Sans SC, TC and KR for Chinese
  and Korean) as `.ttf` or `.otf` in `deps\fonts`; without those, Windows' own fonts (Segoe UI, Microsoft YaHei,
  Microsoft JhengHei, Malgun Gothic) are used. The log says which file each font type got.

## The steps

```
deps       check the Python packages, clang, the Vulkan SDK, SDL3 and the WebView2 SDK
import     your dump -> build/dump (modules as ELF, versions); RomFS and Help read in place   tools/extract/extract.py
functions  every function of each module, with exact boundaries                             tools/extract/functions.py
lift       AArch64 -> C for every function -> build/lift/main                               tools/lifter/recomp.py
compile    the lifted C -> objects (clang -O1, incremental)                                 tools/lifter/build_main.py
tables     generated headers and tables                                       tools/lifter/gen_tables.py, gen_sdktest.py
sdk        the system-library functions that are lifted too                                  tools/lifter/sdklift.py
link       host runtime + game library -> build/bin/smo_native.exe                           tools/lifter/build_exe.py
check      differential test against Unicorn, link check (on demand)        tools/lifter/difftest.py, linkcheck.py
```

A step whose output exists is skipped, so an interrupted setup resumes where it stopped. `compile`, `tables` and `link`
always run and only rebuild what changed. `--status` shows what is done, `--only <step>` runs one step, `--redo <step>`
repeats one, `--from <step>` repeats it and everything after it, `--check` adds the check step (minutes). After a change
to `tools/lifter/sdklift_rules.txt` run `--redo sdk`; after a change to the runtime, `--only link` is enough.

## Running

```bat
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\run.py play --exe smo_native.exe --seconds 0
```

- `smo_native.exe` (and `smo_user.exe`) open a visible window and play sound; `--seconds 0` means no time limit.
- Without `--exe` (the name is then `smo_test.exe`), or with any other name, the run is a test: `scripts\run.py`
  copies `smo_native.exe` to that name, keeps the window hidden (`SMO_SHOW=1` shows it) and silent, and stops the game
  after `--seconds` (default 30). Everything the game prints goes
  to `build\run\<run name>.log`, and a summary (boot stages reached, unimplemented system calls, frames presented, a
  crash with its host frames named) is printed when it ends.
- A test copy first waits while `SMO_MAX_GAMES` test games started this way run on the PC (default: one per 12 GB of
  memory, 2 on a 32 GB PC; `0` = no limit). A game in a stage takes 4-7 GB; more games than fit make the PC page,
  which slows every one of them and can make graphics memory allocations fail.
- `--userdata <folder>` gives the run its own save folder: a new, empty folder starts a new game, a copy of an earlier
  run's folder continues from there. Without it, saves go to `build\userdata\save`.
- `--seq <file>` plays an input sequence (see [`scripted-runs.md`](scripted-runs.md)); `--env NAME=VALUE` sets one of
  the runtime's switches (see [`debugging.md`](debugging.md)).
- Graphics and controller settings live in `build\config\graphics.ini` and `build\config\controllers.ini` (written
  with documented defaults on the first run; `controllers.ini` is read again when you edit it while the game runs).
- The window: by default a borderless window of the size in `graphics.ini`, centred (drag it anywhere to move it). F11,
  or a double-click on it, switches between that and borderless fullscreen; `window = borderless_fullscreen` starts that
  way, and `windowed` (with a title bar) and `fullscreen` (on top) are there too.
- Help (the pause menu's Action Guide) opens inside the game window and the game waits while it is open, as on the
  console: stick or d-pad and A to choose and open, L / R to turn pages, B to go back and to close (keyboard: arrows,
  Enter, Q / E, Escape).
- amiibo: press F1, or both stick buttons of a pad, while you play. The game waits and a menu like its pause menu lists
  the amiibo it knows; up / down (L / R: a page) to choose, A to scan, B (or F1 again) to close. When the game is
  waiting for an amiibo, → is held for you until it has read it; otherwise hold → yourself (the game's amiibo mode)
  and it reads the one you chose. The key and the buttons are set in `controllers.ini`, section `[hotkeys]`.
- The Capture button: F12, or a pad's share button, saves the frame as a BMP in the save folder's `album`.
- Translated shaders are cached in `build\cache\vk`. The first run compiles them as the game meets them and is slower;
  later runs reuse them.

The scripted Cap Kingdom run checks the game from a new save up to Mario's first capture:

```bat
.venv\Scripts\python tests\run_cap_kingdom.py <new run name>
```

It takes about 12 minutes with a warm shader cache (give a first run a larger `--seconds`, e.g. 1500) and exits with
code 0 when every checkpoint was reached and every health counter is zero.

## Troubleshooting

- **A tool is missing:** the `deps` step names it; install it or set the variable it names (`LLVM_ROOT`,
  `VULKAN_HEADERS`, `SDL3_ROOT`, `WEBVIEW2_ROOT`).
- **The import stops:** it names the piece it could not find or that is not what it should be (another game, another
  version, an encrypted file). Check the folder layout above.
- **The first minutes are slow, or loading screens pause:** shaders are being translated and compiled; the cache in
  `build\cache\vk` makes the next run faster.
- **"NOT IMPLEMENTED in the Vulkan back end, skipped" in the log:** an NVN feature the renderer does not have yet; the
  game keeps running, but that part of the picture is not the game's. Please report it with the log.
- **A crash:** the log has a `HOST EXCEPTION` block with the guest function, the registers and the host call stack
  (named from the linker map); `SMO_CRASH_DUMP` and `SMO_WATCH` give more (see [`debugging.md`](debugging.md)).
- **No new frame for 5 seconds:** a watchdog writes every thread's state to the log and to `<exe name>_freeze.txt`.

```

`docs/debugging.md`:

```md
# Debugging aids

The runtime's switches are environment variables with the `SMO_` prefix; pass them to a run with
`scripts\run.py <run name> --env NAME=VALUE`. Everything a run prints goes to `build\run\<run name>.log`.

## The log at a glance

The end of every log has the counts that tell whether a run was healthy:

| Line | Healthy |
|---|---|
| `nvn_vk: N frames presented, ... 0 Vulkan call failures, ... 0 calls of operations that are not implemented` | both zero. An operation the renderer lacks is named once (`NOT IMPLEMENTED in the Vulkan back end, skipped`), counted here and skipped; `SMO_VK_MISSING=exit` stops the game at the first one instead |
| `nvn_vk: images: ...; draws with a geometry stage: ...; indirect: ...` | how often the less common paths ran (storage images, geometry stages, indirect draws and dispatches) |
| `nvn_gl: ... command lists (0 unknown handles) ...` | zero: a non-zero count means draws were dropped (scenery missing or flickering) |
| `nvn: command lists freed: ...` | lists freed when the game finalizes them or records over them; `by the budget` should be 0 |
| `audio: device sink: ... 0 samples dropped ..., 0 underruns ...` | both zero |
| `HOST EXCEPTION` | absent |
| `imports reached ... unimplemented imports reached:` | system calls the game made that have no implementation yet |

## Pictures

- `SMO_SHOT=<n>` saves frame n; `SMO_SHOT_EVERY=<k>` saves every k-th frame from `SMO_SHOT_FROM=<frame>` on (up to
  `SMO_SHOT_TO=<frame>` when given), as `frame_<n>.bmp` in `SMO_SHOT_DIR=<folder>` (the folder must exist).
  `SMO_SHOT_PLAY=<n>` saves the n-th play frame (a frame with compute dispatches and more than 120 draws) as
  `play_<n>.bmp`: the same moment of play whatever the loading took.
- `SMO_VK_PASSSHOT=<frame>` saves colour target 0 at the end of every render pass of that frame
  (`pass_<n>_<format>.bmp`) and logs every draw of it: programs, blend and depth state, viewport, vertex attributes and
  the texture behind every binding. `SMO_VK_PASSSHOT=<first>-<last>/<step>` does it for several frames
  (`pass_<frame>_<n>_<format>.bmp`), for defects that show in some frames only. `SMO_VK_PASSSHOT_RAW=1` adds the
  texels as read, for exact values.
- `SMO_VK_DIAG_NODEPTH=1` draws without depth testing (to see whether something is hidden or missing).
- `SMO_CAPTURE_AT=<frame>[,<frame>...]` presses the Capture button at those frames (the picture goes to the save
  folder's `album`, as when you press F12); `SMO_CAPTURE_GS=<n>` presses it at n frames that drew with a geometry stage
  (the lightning), at least 60 frames apart.
- `SMO_AMIIBO_SHOT_DIR=<folder>` saves the first three different pictures of each opening of the amiibo menu as
  `amiibo_menu_<opening>_<n>.png` (the menu's frames are not game frames, so `SMO_SHOT` does not see them).
- `SMO_GUIDE_SHOT=<file.png>` saves the Help page as shown in the game window (`runtime/game/smo_guide.c`, WebView2) 1.5 s
  after it loaded and 0.8 s after each pad action, as `<file>_2.png`, `_3.png`, ... (at most 8); `SMO_SHOT` does not see
  it either. The log says what the guide does (`guide:`).

## Shaders

- Translated stages are cached in `build\cache\vk` (`SMO_VK_CACHE=<folder>` uses another one; an empty folder forces
  every stage to be translated again).
- `SMO_VK_GLSLDUMP=<folder>` writes the GLSL of every stage translated in the run.
- `SMO_SHADERDUMP=<folder>` writes the machine code of stages that could not be translated (`vk_fail_*.bin`); with
  `SMO_VK_DUMP_MINBYTES=<n>` (stages whose GLSL is at least n bytes) or `SMO_VK_DUMP_SERIAL=<n>` (one program; serials
  change from run to run) it writes `vk_prog_*.bin` for the equivalence harness. `tools\dev\mxdis.py <file.bin>` names
  the instructions of a dump.
- `SMO_MX_NOSTRUCT=1` translates with the old `switch(pc)` control flow instead of structured blocks;
  `SMO_MX_MUTATE=1` plants a known bug, to check that the equivalence harness catches it.
- Equivalence harness: `tests\build_mx_equiv.py`, then from `build\bin`: `mx_equiv.exe <folder of vk_prog_*.bin> [max]`.
- `tests\check_all_shaders.py` takes every shader stage out of the game's shader archives (agl `.sharcb`, g3d `.bfsha`,
  the effect `.ptcl`, nested archives, `main` and `sdk`) into `build\shaders_all`, translates each with the Vulkan back
  end's settings and compiles it with the renderer's compiler; `--list` adds a line per stage, `--extract-only` stops
  after the extraction. A geometry stage is checked for point, line and triangle input.
- `SMO_VK_GS_DEBUG=<mode>` for draws with a geometry stage: `1` measures them (`nvn_vk_gs:` lines: the GPU's pipeline
  statistics of 16 of them, and the colour target read back before and after every 20th, which says how many pixels
  each draw brightened and by how much), `2` leaves them out (to compare pictures), `3` draws them in bright magenta
  without the depth test and measures them as 1 does.

## Missing or flickering draws

- Check the `unknown handles` count first. `SMO_CMDMEMLOG=1` logs the command memory the game hands to its command
  buffers (the first 400 times), which decides when a recorded list is over.
- `SMO_LIST_BUDGET_MB=<n>` (default 4096) is a last-resort limit on recorded command lists; when it drops lists it says
  so, because the game may still submit them.
- `SMO_TEXLOG=1` logs texture creation, finalization and registration; the per-draw log of `SMO_VK_PASSSHOT` says why
  a texture handle is unknown (slot outside the pool, never registered, or a texture that was finalized).
- Graphics memory: the `nvn_vk: totals` line (every 600 frames) ends with the device memory the renderer has allocated
  and the images of textures nothing names any more that were freed (agl gave up every texture pool slot of the
  texture and the object that made it holds another one; `runtime/gfx/nvn_gl.c`, above `pool_ent_release`). Such an image
  goes after `SMO_VK_TEXFREE=<frames>` unused frames (default 8; `0` keeps every image, as before). `made again` counts
  textures used after their image went (what the GPU had drawn into one is lost then; it should stay 0, and
  `nvn_vk_tex:` lines name them). With `SMO_TEXLOG=1` every release of a slot and every freed image is logged too.
- Flicker that shows in single frames: save every frame of a stretch (`SMO_SHOT_EVERY=1 SMO_SHOT_FROM=<a> SMO_SHOT_TO=<b>
  SMO_SHOT_DIR=<folder>`), then `tools\dev\flicker.py <folder>` lists the frames where a region of the picture is brighter
  or darker than in both neighbours, and saves them side by side. To see what such a frame drew differently, run the same
  stretch again with `SMO_VK_PASSSHOT=<a>-<b> SMO_VK_PASSSHOT_LOGONLY=1 SMO_VK_FRAMELOG=<a>-<b>` (every draw logged,
  no pass pictures; a lot of log) and `tools\dev\drawdiff.py build\run\<name>.log <frame>`: the draws the frame has that
  neither neighbour has, and the ones it lacks.
- `SMO_VK_FRAMELOG=<first>-<last>`: one `nvn_vk_frame:` line per frame (draws, draws left out and why, conditional
  renders, render passes, texture barriers, stream ring wraps and kilobytes streamed).

## Speed

- Every 300 frames the log has `nvn_perf: frames A..B frame time ms: ...` (frame times, fps, 1% low), `nvn_perf: cpu
  ms/frame by thread` and `nvn_vk_perf:` (where the render thread's time went: batch replay, draw preparation, waits for
  the GPU, present). `nvn_texhash:` says how many textures were checked for changes by hashing their memory, and why.
- `nvn_vk_frames:` at exit counts the frames that drew a scene, i.e. had compute dispatches (in the Cap Kingdom run 40,164
  of 42,589; the others are boot and loading frames). Within 600 frames of such a frame the renderer does not hold the
  game's threads for its workers and makes only cheap textures ahead of their use; in a frame that draws a scene its
  workers run below normal priority.
- `SMO_HOSTPROF=<start s>,<seconds>[,<threads>][;<start s>,<seconds>[,<threads>] ...]` samples the stacks of the
  busiest threads (default 4) about every millisecond in each window and prints the functions met most often, what
  each thread was blocked in, and under which function of the game. `tools\dev\profnames.py build\run\<name>.log` adds
  the names of the lifted game's functions (`guest f_...`) from the function list.
- `SMO_FRAMETL=<first frame>,<frames>` records a timeline of those frames (every job the game's threads queue for the
  render thread and when it ran, the submissions to the GPU and the waits for it, the presents, the game's waits for the
  refresh and the refreshes, each with its thread and processor) into `SMO_FRAMETL_OUT=<file>` (default `frametl.txt`
  next to the exe). `tools\dev\frametl.py <file>` makes a table of it per frame: when the batch was submitted, how long
  the replay and the present took and how much of it was waiting for the GPU, how long the main thread drew after the
  present, and how far ahead of the next refresh it was done; the slow frames are listed.
- `nvn_vk_ring:` (every 300 frames) says what the stream ring copied per frame, how often its range caches were dropped
  (`new generations`) and which writes of the host into guest memory were checked against them instead.
- `tools\dev\cpuload.py --busy <n> --seconds <s> --log <file>` keeps n processes busy (arithmetic and memory copies) and
  logs the CPU use of the system, the game and the busiest other programs every 5 seconds: frame rates measured while
  other programs use the PC, the same way each time.
- `SMO_PRIORITY_CLASS=normal` runs the process in the NORMAL priority class (default ABOVE_NORMAL: the game's threads
  are tied to three processors and must come before other programs' threads there; `runtime/os/os_threads.c`).
- `SMO_FAST=0` leaves the game's own code where `runtime/game/smo_fast.c` puts host code in its place (the sort of the
  sampler list of `agl::driver::NVNMgr`); `SMO_FAST_CHECK=1` runs the game's code as well and stops the game if the
  results ever differ. The game's `main` has no symbols for these functions: `tools/lifter/gen_tables.py` finds them
  by matching the base executable's (in `build\dump\base`), and the log says so when the fast path stays off.
- Switches that bring back an older behaviour, for comparisons: `SMO_VK_OCC_SYNC=1` (every occlusion report waits for the
  GPU), `SMO_VK_OCC_PRESENT=0` (occlusion results are not waited for at the present), `SMO_VK_RING_DRAIN=1` (the stream
  ring waits for the GPU at every wrap), `SMO_TEXHASH_ALL=1` (textures are hashed whatever their memory pool),
  `SMO_VK_NO_TEXBARRIER=1` (the game's fragment-order barriers are ignored), `SMO_SYNC_SUBMIT=1` (every submit waits for
  the render thread), `SMO_VK_VTXGROW=0` (vertex streams are copied only as far as the range the game bound, even when
  the draw reads further; `SMO_VK_VTXCHECK=1` logs each kind of draw that does). `SMO_PRESENT_ASYNC=1` lets the present not wait for the render thread (one frame in flight);
  `SMO_VK_OCC_LOG=1` logs the conditional renders that had to wait for an occlusion result.

## Memory

- Every 300 frames the log has `nvn_vk_mem: frame F:` the process's working set (its private part and peak), private
  bytes, the commit of pagefile-backed sections (the game's memory heap), the Vulkan memory the renderer allocated (the
  host-visible part is system memory the driver keeps resident) and the shader modules made, released and made again.
- `tools\dev\memmap.py <pid or exe name> [--log build\run\<name>.log] [--zero 64] [--json <file>]` reads a
  running game from outside (nothing is written into it): every allocation with its reserved, committed and resident
  size, named where it can be (images and mapped files, thread stacks with their start function from the exe's map, NT
  heap segments and large blocks, the guest memory heap and NVN virtual pools from the log, Vulkan memory blocks with
  `SMO_VK_MEMLOG=1`). `--zero` adds, for the large allocations, how much of what is resident holds only zeros and where
  in the allocation it lies.
- Where a game's memory goes (Sand Kingdom home stage, frame 6000 of a scripted run): the game's own memory heap
  (2.2 GB resident of the 3.05 GB the game asks for; 92% of it non-zero data), the graphics driver's heaps (stage
  libraries and pipelines, the pipeline cache object: 640 MB), the stream ring (256 MB of resident system memory), the C
  runtime heap (250 MB), executables and DLLs (100 MB). Graphics memory adds commit, not resident memory: about as much
  as the Vulkan memory, for the driver's eviction backing.
- `SMO_VK_MODREL=0` keeps every shader module (by default a stage's module is released once its pipeline library or
  compute pipeline is made, and made again from the stage cache's SPIR-V file if needed: 1.1 GB less).
- `SMO_VK_PCACHE=0` makes pipelines without a pipeline cache object (nothing read or saved): 640 MB less, as fast for an
  exe the driver has run before, but the NVIDIA driver keeps its own shader cache per executable, so an exe under a new
  name compiles everything again.

## Crashes and stalls

- A crash prints `HOST EXCEPTION` with the last guest function, its registers and the host call stack, named from the
  linker map next to the exe. `SMO_CRASH_DUMP=<bytes>` (0x60 to 0x1000) adds memory at every register, the strings it
  finds there and the guest's frame-pointer chain (the real guest call stack).
- `SMO_WATCH=<heap offset>[,<length>]` logs every write that changes that range of the game's heap, with the writing
  function (heap offsets repeat from run to run).
- No presented frame for 5 seconds writes every thread's state (locks, waits, call stacks) to the log and to
  `<exe name>_freeze.txt` (`SMO_VK_WATCHDOG=<seconds>`, 0 = off). `SMO_VK_BARRIER_DUMP=1` prints every thread's stack
  when a loading barrier times out.

## The game's state

- `SMO_NERVELOG=<substrings>` prints every change of state of the game's state machines whose state name contains one of
  them (`*` = all): `nerve: frame F keeper K: OpeningStageStartDemoNrvCameraAuto -> OpeningStageStartDemoNrvCameraTutorial`.
- `SMO_ACTORPOS=<n>[:<state name prefixes>]` prints actor positions every n frames (default: the player).
- `SMO_ICALLS=<start second>,<seconds>` counts the targets of indirect calls in that window and prints them at the time
  limit; map the `f_71...` addresses with `build\functions\main_functions.tsv` (address - 0x7100000000). Every state
  machine runs its current state once a frame through such a call, so the active one stands out.
- See [`scripted-runs.md`](scripted-runs.md) for waiting on states and steering in input sequences.

## Audio and input

- `SMO_AUDIO=0` turns the audio output off; `SMO_AUDIO_WAV=<file>` also writes the final mix to a WAV file.
- Test copies (any exe name but `smo_native.exe` and `smo_user.exe`) are silent: their volume in the Windows mixer is
  0. The sound is still made and fed to the device as with sound, so the timing, the dropped-sample and underrun counts
  and an `SMO_AUDIO_WAV` capture are the same. `SMO_VOLUME=<0..100>` sets the volume of any copy (the log says
  `host volume N%`).
- `SMO_HIDLOG=1` logs the pad values the game reads, when they change.
- `SMO_PAD_SELFTEST=1` runs the controller self-test with SDL3 virtual devices and exits.
- amiibo: the log says when the menu opens and closes (`amiibo menu:`), what the NFC reader does (`nfp:` an amiibo held to
  it, found when the game searches, its model information read by the game, taken away) and whether → is held for the
  game (`nn::hid:`). `SMO_NERVELOG=HelpAmiibo` shows the game's amiibo mode (Wait, CountHold, Active, IconClose).

## Starting elsewhere in the game

- `tools\dev\save_warp.py <save folder> --out <new folder> --stage <StageName> [--world <n>] [--scenario <n>]
  [--checkpoint <object id> --visited]` copies a save folder so that its game file continues in another stage (at the
  stage's default entrance, for a kingdom the Odyssey; the world number comes from `SystemData\WorldList.szs` for a
  kingdom's home stage, e.g. `BossRaidWorldHomeStage` = 11). `--scenario` sets the kingdom's scenario (which objects
  its stages place); `--checkpoint` starts at one of the stage's checkpoint flags (`tools\dev\byml.py
  StageData\<Stage>Map.szs --grep CheckpointFlag` lists them; the flag is marked as reached in the copy, a flag in a
  zone is named `<id>(<zone>[<the zone's id in the stage>])`), `--reached <object id>` marks more flags as reached
  without starting at them, and `--visited` lets it apply in a kingdom the save has
  not been to (a first visit starts at the Odyssey). Run it with `scripts\run.py <name> --userdata <new folder>`: a late
  kingdom can be tried without playing to it. The source folder is only read; never give your own save folder as
  `--out`.
- A save always resumes in a kingdom's home stage. `SMO_START_STAGE=<stage>[:<scenario>]` (TEST ONLY) makes the first
  stage scene the game starts that stage instead, at its default start point, as when Mario goes through its entrance:
  any sub-area, room or 2D section (the log says `start stage: frame F: the game starts <home>, scenario N;
  SMO_START_STAGE makes it <stage>, scenario M (<whose>)`). Give it a save warped to the stage's kingdom. The runtime
  watches for `StageScene::init` (found in the game's own vtable, `GAME_VSYM_StageScene_init` in `build\gen\image.h`)
  and changes the stage name it is called with, once; later stage scenes are only logged (`the game starts <stage>,
  scenario <n> itself`, e.g. the restart after a miss). The scenario: the one given (`asked for`), else the stage's own
  when the game has one for it (`the stage's own, as through its door`: what the game's own `ChangeStageInfo` gives a
  stage when no scenario is asked for, as the doors to sub-areas do; 1 for a kingdom's challenge rooms), else the
  kingdom's as the game chose it (`the kingdom's`). A stage that follows the kingdom's scenario can still be started in one whose home map has no door to it (the Mushroom Kingdom shop in
  scenario 1 shows the game's unbaked placeholder lighting): choosing such a scenario is not done yet. Starting a
  cutscene stage this way, out of its order, can meet game code that expects the story to be where that cutscene
  belongs.
- `SMO_STAGE_LIST=<stage>[:<scenario>[:<start>]],...` (TEST ONLY) plays several stages one after another in one run, so
  that a test of many stages boots the game once. The first is the stage the run starts in (the save's, or
  `SMO_START_STAGE`'s). Each time the input sequence (`SMO_SEQ`) is done, the game changes to the next stage of the list
  through its own stage change, the one a door makes: at the scene's next `StageSceneNrvPlay` (while it waits, B is
  pressed every 45 polls: a map, the pause menu or a message the sequence left open would hold it) the runtime has the
  game make a `ChangeStageInfo` (its own constructor) for the stage, the scenario (default: the game's choice, as for a door)
  and the start point (the id of a placed start, e.g. a checkpoint flag's `PlayerRestartPos` link; default: the stage's
  default start), and hands it to `GameDataFunction::tryChangeNextStage`; the scene then ends and the game loads the
  stage, a kingdom's home stage with its kingdom. The game's `main` has no symbols for the two functions: they are
  matched with the base executable's (`GAME_FN_*` in `build\gen\image.h`, see `find_func` in
  `tools\lifter\gen_tables.py`). When the
  stage's `StageScene::init` runs, the input sequence starts again: `SMO_SEQ_<n>` for the n-th stage of the list
  (counted from 1), else `SMO_STAGE_SEQ`, else `SMO_SEQ`. The log marks each stage: `stage list: frame F: stage n of N
  begins: the game starts <stage>, scenario <s>`, then `stage list: stage n of N done at frame F (poll P): run totals:
  ...`, the counters of the end-of-run summary so far (frames presented, Vulkan call failures, operations not
  implemented, imports and stubs, audio dropped and underruns, loading-screen holds, process memory, run time), so a test
  can take them apart per stage. After the last stage the run ends as with `SMO_SEQ_EXIT=1`. The run's time limit (the
  exe's second argument) counts from the start of the stage being played. Stay within one kingdom: the game changes
  kingdom for a home stage only, so another kingdom's sub-area would load with the old kingdom's scenario.
- `tests\stress_stages.py --save <save folder> [--scenarios] [--jobs 2] [--speed 4] [--cache <folder>]`
  starts every stage of the game from a warped copy of the save (a kingdom's home stage directly, any other stage with
  `SMO_START_STAGE`; with `--scenarios` also every scenario of every kingdom, at its checkpoint flags), plays a few
  seconds of each at a raised speed and lists what the logs show: host exceptions, the game's aborts, operations not
  implemented, shader stages not translated, Vulkan failures, unimplemented system calls, freezes, dummy textures,
  stages that never reach play (`build\stress\<name>\summary.md`, with four small pictures a run). It also
  uses two test switches: `SMO_SPEED=<n>` (TEST ONLY) runs the refresh clock n times faster, 60 x n refreshes a second
  (0 = 960): the game steps once per refresh, so it runs up to n times faster where the PC keeps up, and input sequences,
  counted in frames, play the same; `SMO_SEQ_EXIT=1` ends the run when its input sequence is done. A game takes about
  6 GB of memory: two jobs fit a 32 GB PC with other programs open, and `scripts\run.py` makes a job wait while
  `SMO_MAX_GAMES` test games run on the PC ([`building.md`](building.md)). About three quarters of a run's frames come before play
  (the boot to the title menu alone is about half), so short runs spend most of their time starting. `--chain N` plays
  up to N stages of one kingdom and one kind (stages in the save's scenario; scenarios started at a checkpoint flag;
  scenarios at their default start) in one run with `SMO_STAGE_LIST`, splits the log per stage
  (`build\run\<name>_<stage>.log`, as a run of its own is named) and records each stage as its own run would,
  its counters from the run's totals after each stage; after a crash or a time limit a new run plays the stages left.
  `--exe-prefix` names the jobs' exe copies. A stage that only a painting leads to (the Mushroom Kingdom's six boss
  rematches, the Darker Side's last room; found in the maps: its `MissRestartArea` names the room, whose
  `PictureStageChange` leads to it) is entered as in play: its run starts in the painting's room and changes to the
  stage with the painting's `ChangeStageName` and `ChangeStageId`. Started directly (`--direct`, for comparisons), the
  restart after a miss goes to that room before the kingdom's resource loader has its archives, and they overflow the
  restart's 512 KB scene resource heap (`nn::diag abort` on FileLoadThread); in play the room is entered first and its
  archives are already in the kingdom's heap. Restarts the game makes itself are logged (`the game starts <stage>,
  scenario <n> itself`) and listed per stage (`restarts` in `results.jsonl`).

## Other switches

- Threads: the game's three console cores run on three processors of the PC, one per physical core, from a slot of six
  processors the game takes for itself: counted from the top of the process's affinity, the first slot no other
  running game holds (a named mutex per slot, `Local\smo_console_cores_<k>`; a 32-processor PC has five). A game alone
  takes slot 0; games started while it runs take the next ones, so games side by side never share these processors
  (`console cores in processor slot K of N` in the log). `SMO_OS_HOST_CPUS=<hexadecimal mask>` chooses the processors
  instead (the stress test's `--cpus split`). TEST ONLY, for comparisons: `SMO_OS_PRIO17=0` puts the game's priority 17 back on one level with
  18 to 27 (by default the model draw buffer update, 17, runs before the archive decompression, 18, as on the console).
- `SMO_IMPORT_SELFTEST=1` checks the system calls implemented from the list of the game's imports rather than met in
  play (C library, threads and message queues, files, C++ library pieces, `nn::util`, diagnostics and time, the web
  applet, the NFC reader with an amiibo held to it, the amiibo menu's list and picture): run when every handler is
  registered, before the game starts; one line per group, then it exits with the number of failed checks as exit code.
  `SMO_AMIIBO_SHOT=<file.png>` also saves the menu picture it composes.
- `SMO_MANUAL=<folder>` takes the game's manual from that folder instead of `build\manual`; `SMO_WEB_NOOPEN=1` prepares
  the Help pages without showing them (neither in the game window nor in the browser).
- `SMO_STRICT=1` lists, at start, every import bound to a handler that does nothing and every function import without a
  handler, and stops (exit code 5); `SMO_STRICT=report` lists them and goes on. The `strict check:` line of every log
  counts them.
- `SMO_VK_CSLOG=1` logs compute dispatches with large work groups.
- `SMO_USERDATA=<folder>` is the save folder (`scripts\run.py --userdata` sets it).
- `SMO_SDK_SELFTEST=1` runs the self-test of the service families (`runtime/services/nnservices.c`); it fails two
  checks (the `errno` location, `NumberLineAllocator` not lifted) and stops at `nn::image::JpegDecoder`, a game import
  without a handler.

## Looking things up in the executable

- `tools\dev\disasm.py <symbol or address> [--module main|sdk]` disassembles one function, naming call targets.
- `tools\dev\callers.py <name substring>` lists the callers of a function or import.
- `tools\dev\sarc.py <romfs path>` lists the files in a SARC archive of the extracted RomFS;
  `tools\dev\byml.py StageData\<Stage>Map.szs --scenario 0 --grep <name>` lists the objects placed in a stage, with
  their positions (prints to the console only).
- `tools\lifter\mapaddr.py` names host addresses from the linker map.
- The function list (`build\functions\<module>_functions.tsv`) names functions by the module's own symbols (column
  `symbol`) and, for `main`, the `execute` function of every state class from its RTTI (column `rtti_name`): the
  game's `main` keeps almost no symbols, so these are most of its names. `tools\target.py` says where the build's
  files are.

```

`docs/scripted-runs.md`:

```md
# Scripted runs

A scripted run plays the game with no input but a sequence file, and checks what happened against the game's own
state. It is how gameplay is tested here: the same sequence, played after a change, must still reach the same
checkpoints. `tests/run_cap_kingdom.py` is the example: from an empty save to Mario's first capture in Top-Hat Tower.

```bat
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\run.py <run name> --seconds 600 --seq tests\cap_kingdom.seq --userdata build\run\<run name>_save
```

## Sequences

A sequence (`SMO_SEQ`; `--seq <file>` reads it from a file, `#` starts a comment) is a list of steps, executed in order
and counted in pad polls (the game polls player 1 once per frame), so it does not depend on how long loading took:

| Step | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<n>` | wait n polls |
| `<n>:<keys>[/<h>]` | wait n polls, then hold the keys for h polls (default 8) |
| `@nerve:<state>` | wait until the game runs that state, e.g. `@nerve:OpeningStageStartDemoNrvWaitStandUp` |
| `@until-nerve:<state>:<keys>/<p>` | press the keys every p polls until the state runs (e.g. advance a talk until play resumes) |
| `@goto:<x>,<z>[,<r>][/<n>]` | steer the left stick to the world point (x, z) until the player is within r (default 100), at most n polls |
| `@near:<state prefix>[,<r>][/<n>]` | steer to the nearest actor whose state starts with the prefix until within r (default 250); the player then faces it |
| `@at:<x>,<y>,<z>[,<r>]` | wait until the player is within r (default 300) of the point, e.g. where a new stage puts him |
| `@chase:<state prefix>[,<r>]/<n>` | for n polls, follow that actor, standing still within r (for exploring) |
| `@draws:<lo>-<hi>[/<n>]` | wait until n frames in a row had between lo and hi draw calls (a screen recognised by its draw count) |
| `@until:<lo>-<hi>[/<n>]:<keys>/<p>` | press the keys every p polls until the draw count is in that range |
| `@movie` | wait until a movie is opened |

Keys: `Z` `X` `C` `V` = A B X Y, `Q` `E` = L R, `A` `S` = ZL ZR, `!` = Plus, `-` = Minus, `I` `J` `K` `L` = d-pad
up/left/down/right, `u` `d` `l` `r` = left stick, `8` `2` `4` `6` = right stick up/down/left/right, `*` = the amiibo
menu's key. Every step is announced in the log with its poll and frame number.

While the amiibo menu is open the game is held, but the sequence goes on, one poll per frame of the menu: for example
`@nerve:StageSceneNrvPlay 240 1:* 30 1:E/4 20 1:Z 900` opens it, moves a page down (to Peach), chooses it and lets the
game read it (the log's `amiibo menu:`, `nfp:` and `nn::hid:` lines say what happened).

## The game's state

Every state machine of the game is an `al::NerveKeeper`: its current state (a "nerve") runs once a frame through a call
the runtime sees (`runtime/game/smo_nerve.c`). A state's name is the game's own class name for it, for example
`StageSceneNrvPlay` or `OpeningStageStartDemoNrvCameraTutorial`. Names come from the function list
(`build\functions\main_functions.tsv`): the class names the game's RTTI gives. The tracker names the others from the
code: a state whose
code calls `<Class>::exe<State>()` is `<Class>Nrv<State>`, one that runs a sub-state is named after its neighbours,
`<Class>Nrv_<address>`. Many classes are called `HostTypeNrv<State>` by the game itself (one per actor class); such a
state gets the class of the object that first runs it: `FrogNrvWait`.

- `SMO_NERVELOG=*` (or a list of substrings) logs every change of state with its frame number: the first thing to run
  when a scripted run gets stuck.
- `SMO_ACTORPOS=<n>[:<prefixes>]` logs where actors are (the player by default); following another actor's path, such as
  Cappy running ahead in the opening, gives waypoints that are known to be walkable.
- `SMO_ICALLS=<start>,<seconds>` counts which functions run in a window; the state that runs every frame stands out.
- The tracker costs time on every indirect call. It is on when a sequence has a step that needs it (`@nerve`,
  `@until-nerve`, `@goto`, `@near`, `@at`, `@chase`) and stops by itself once no such step is left, unless
  `SMO_NERVELOG` or `SMO_ACTORPOS` asks for it; so a timing run that only waits for a state at the start runs at full
  speed after it (the log says `nerve: tracking stops at frame F`).

## Steering

`@goto` turns a world direction into a stick direction the way the game does: it reads the game's camera (position and
look-at point), takes its forward direction on the ground plane as stick up and its right as stick right, and corrects
every poll, so the camera may turn while Mario runs. When the player moves less than 30 units in 12 polls, the step
holds A for 14 polls (a jump, enough for a step up), then waits 10 polls before it may jump again. A step ends early
when a cutscene takes the player for 10 polls, and when a new stage starts (a new player object).

## Finding a route

- The stage's placement data has the paths the game's own route guide shows: `tools\dev\byml.py
  StageData\<Stage>Map.szs --scenario 0 --grep RouteGuide` lists the objects; their rail points (in the BYML) are good
  waypoints.
- Doors, switches and moving parts often need something before they let Mario through. Their code says what: in Cap
  Kingdom the way down to Top-Hat Tower rises only after a cap hits the `CapSwitchSave`, and the tower door opens only
  on a cap hit (`DoorAreaChange::receiveMsg`); a `V` (Y, throw) facing the object does it.
- A copy of an earlier run's save folder (`--userdata`) starts from the last autosave, which makes trying the next part
  of a route quicker than starting from a new game every time.

## The Cap Kingdom run

`tests\run_cap_kingdom.py <new run name>` plays `tests\cap_kingdom.seq` from an empty save and checks 13 checkpoints:

1. the mode select of a new game
2. the prologue skipped through its own menu (Plus twice, then Skip)
3. the opening's camera tutorial passed: it ends when the camera looks more than 60 degrees away from straight down,
   so the right stick tilts it
4. Mario stands up
5. gameplay begins
6. Cappy reached on the bridge after his three runs
7. Cappy joins: the cap-throw tutorial
8. the cap thrown
9. Bonneton's stairs climbed
10. the cap switch hit and the path risen
11. the tower door opened by the cap
12. inside Top-Hat Tower (a new stage)
13. a frog captured

It also requires 0 host exceptions, 0 Vulkan call failures, 0 operations not implemented, 0 unknown command handles,
and no dropped audio samples or underruns. It takes about 12 minutes with a warm shader cache. The checkpoints land on
the same frames within a few frames from run to run.

Limits: the route depends on the game behaving the same way each time (it does, as far as measured); the sequence
does not avoid enemies (a small Goomba hits Mario once on the way to the tower door).
